subtitle: Assess each area with evidence, then choose the next practice.
summary: One cinema team automates rightsizing, and someone proposes an “Inspiring” badge for the whole organization. Pip asks what the other teams can demonstrate. The book’s Green Software Maturity Matrix describes five levels—Aspiring, Aware, Acting, Awesome, and Inspiring—across several axes. Training, inventories, and manual cleanup can begin the journey; repeatable processes, broader measurement, automation, and dynamic electricity response develop later. Operations, product management, device support, and education may advance unevenly. This is the supplied 2024 framework, not a current certification. Pip uses it to choose an evidenced next practice, not reward an ambitious label.

concepts.title: A maturity model guides improvement
concepts.body: Pip reaches for the highest badge, then opens the evidence folder. The maturity matrix describes practices and next steps, not an award earned by enthusiasm. Its five levels move from interest toward repeatable work and quantitative improvement, giving leaders and advocates a shared vocabulary. Pip brings inventory and recurring review records instead of an aspiration. The criteria belong to the book’s version; this learning exercise does not issue a certification.

steps.text: Pip checks the evidence before choosing a level.
Use the book’s framework to choose the next action, not issue certification.

concepts.title: Early action does not require perfect telemetry
concepts.body: The cinema wants perfect real-time telemetry before touching an idle environment. Pip proposes a reviewed inventory and cleanup while the baseline improves. Early practice can use retrospective data and qualified proxies to rightsize resources, choose suitable hosting, and build operational skills. The book encourages starting from actual capability. Elaborate measurement may help later, but it need not delay action on visible waste whose owners and recovery needs can already be checked.

steps.text: Pip starts from the organization’s actual capability.
An unused environment is already visible.
Improve measurement while acting with transparent evidence.

concepts.title: Repeatability separates pilots from practice
concepts.body: Pip’s pilot clears a room of unused workers. Next month, another team recreates them. A successful project is not yet a repeatable practice. The Acting level emphasizes defined processes, broader emissions knowledge, recurring review, product waste, and device longevity; later levels add automation and quantitative response. Pip assigns owners, documents scope, schedules reviews, and records exceptions. The evidence must show the practice happens beyond one memorable cleanup.

steps.text: Pip notices waste return after a successful trial.
A pilot proves a technique in one scope.
Recurring review and exception evidence establish repeatability.

concepts.title: Assess axes independently
concepts.body: The operations team celebrates repeatable rightsizing, but nobody owns older-phone support. Pip draws separate columns rather than averaging the gap away. The matrix covers commitments, footprint, metrics, operations, electricity, end-user devices, servers, product management, and education. Different owners may have different capabilities. Strong server practice cannot establish a missing device policy. Recording each axis’s evidence and uncertainty gives Pip a more useful next step than an unsupported overall score.

steps.text: Pip refuses to hide an uneven picture.
Assess evidence independently across the matrix’s axes.

concepts.title: Distinguish annual claims from continuous response
concepts.body: A poster promises renewable electricity over a year. Pip asks for the time and place of actual operation. Higher maturity envisions real-time and forecast data, budgets, and use matched to carbon-free supply by interval and location. Annual purchases or future commitments do not demonstrate that capability. Pip records the claim under commitments and seeks operational evidence separately. The book’s matrix also focuses on greenhouse-gas-related software practice, not every environmental concern.

steps.text: Pip separates a commitment from operational capability.
An annual purchase does not describe every operating hour.
Continuous matching needs evidence beyond the annual claim.

misconceptions.claim: One advanced team proves the whole organization is advanced.
misconceptions.correction: Record the scope of evidence separately across teams and axes. A pilot does not establish a consistent practice.

misconceptions.claim: A maturity level is a measured emissions reduction.
misconceptions.correction: A level describes practices and evidence. Actual resource and emissions outcomes need their own measurements.

scenario.title: An honest maturity review
scenario.context: Pip reviews a cinema company with one rightsizing pilot, an annual emissions report, and keen volunteers. Other teams still provision manually; older-device support has no policy. Leaders need an honest next-quarter plan using the book’s matrix, not a badge based on the strongest team.

options.label: Assess each axis and expand one repeatable practice
options.benefit: Makes gaps visible and turns a demonstrated technique into an achievable next step.
options.cost: Requires gathering evidence from several owners and accepting an uneven picture.
options.consequence: The review records the platform pilot’s scope and assigns a broader operating process. Device-support work remains a separate gap with an owner.

options.label: Invest first in shared real-time measurement
options.benefit: Could improve feedback for later quantitative decisions.
options.cost: Does not itself standardize operations or resolve unsupported devices.
options.consequence: The team defines what decisions the new data would enable, while making clear that instrumentation is not proof of maturity on every axis.

scenario.debrief: The next investment should follow the bottleneck revealed by evidence. More detailed data can be useful without being the only path forward.

quiz.question: A pilot auto-scales well but the rest of the company does not. What should the assessment record?
options: The pilot’s scope and the remaining adoption gap
quiz.explanation: The matrix distinguishes actual organizational practice from isolated capability.

quiz.question: Which is a reasonable early improvement with incomplete carbon data?
options: Review and rightsize unused allocation using consistent evidence
quiz.explanation: Useful early action can proceed with transparent proxies and operational checks.

quiz.question: What does an annual renewable-energy purchase alone fail to demonstrate?
options: That the organization made a commitment
quiz.explanation: Annual accounting does not establish the time-and-place matching described in the higher-level vision.

exercise.title: Assess two maturity axes
exercise.prompt: Use the book’s framework to assess two areas you influence. Keep evidence, missing information, and aspirations separate. Choose one achievable next practice.

fields.label: Axes and current evidence
fields.placeholder: Which operations, metrics, device, product, or education practices can you demonstrate?

fields.label: Gaps and scope
fields.placeholder: Which teams or capabilities remain unverified or inconsistent?

fields.label: Next practice and review
fields.placeholder: Who will establish the next repeatable action, and what evidence will show it happened?

steps.text: Pip refuses to hide an uneven picture.
Assess evidence independently across the matrix’s axes.

title: The Green Software Maturity Matrix
